       1             SENATOR BALL:  Good morning.

       2             If we could just start with the Pledge of

       3      Allegiance, everybody, and then we'll get started.

       4             I pledge allegiance to the flag of the

       5      United States of America, and to the Republic for

       6      which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible,

       7      with liberty and justice for all.

       8             I know that everybody is busy, so we're going

       9      to get started.

      10             We have a few more senators that are on their

      11      way, and making it to the North Country from the

      12      city, which can always be tough.  I know, in the

      13      reverse direction, I am late sometimes.

      14             I want to introduce Senator Krueger for a

      15      couple brief remarks.

      16             Before that, I'll just make a brief

      17      statement.

      18             You know, we're on the precipice of having a

      19      multi-billion dollar industry come in to the state

      20      of New York.

      21             And as a legislator, sometimes you sit at a

      22      table.  And specifically on this issue, those who

      23      are against fracking, very successfully, and very

      24      forcefully, present their side, their opinion.  And

      25      then the industry --





 

                                                                   5
       1             Senator, how are you?

       2             SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:  Hi.

       3             SENATOR BALL:  -- then the industry will,

       4      with an absolute certainty, present their side.

       5             And at the end of that discussion, you're

       6      left scratching your heads, saying:  Who's telling

       7      the truth, and where's the gray here.

       8             I find that, in politics, the answer isn't

       9      always on the extreme of either side.  But in this

      10      one, we're dealing with folks' health, the quality

      11      of our environment, and some extremely pressing

      12      issues.

      13             So, I decided to head to Pennsylvania, right

      14      across the border, and see it firsthand.

      15             And I can tell you that I saw some good

      16      stuff.  I saw some economic activity, I saw some job

      17      creation.  Some of those jobs were from -- for folks

      18      from Texas and Colorado, not Pennsylvanians, which

      19      is a totally different issue.

      20             But, I saw some bad stuff too.  Some really

      21      bad stuff.

      22             I saw farmers whose lives were devastated;

      23      whose cattle, in one instance, there were

      24      eleven cows at freshen.

      25             Many of you may not have grown up on a farm.





 

                                                                   6
       1      I did.

       2             Out of those eleven, eight of those were

       3      still-birth.  The farmer was pulling dead calves out

       4      of those cows.

       5             Eight out of eleven -- if any you have an

       6      agricultural background -- is absolutely ridiculous.

       7      Just doesn't happen.

       8             I saw a fifth-generation family, whose

       9      property value went from $300,000 to $9,000.  Their

      10      water was contaminated.

      11             And the industry said, "Well, it's not our

      12      fault"; even though they had been drinking that

      13      water from five generations.  And only in the

      14      aftermath of a fracking platform put on a neighbor's

      15      property was their water contaminated.

      16             And I've seen loophole after loophole in

      17      Pennsylvania, where an industry has been allowed to

      18      walk through those loopholes with nothing short of a

      19      Mack truck.

      20             Can we frack in New York?  Can we create jobs

      21      in New York?  Can we increase economic activity in

      22      New York?

      23             Let's have that discussion, but let's not do

      24      it by creating the very same loopholes that we've

      25      seen taken advantage of in other states.





 

                                                                   7
       1             I invited the industry to come here today --

       2                  [Applause.]

       3             SENATOR BALL:  I invited the industry to come

       4      here today.

       5             And, honestly, there were questions, with the

       6      hearing that held when I was in the Assembly, that I

       7      really would have liked to have had answers, to.

       8             I think it's extremely important that we dig

       9      down into this issue as New Yorkers on both sides of

      10      the aisle, and really begin to ask some of the very

      11      tough questions that need to be had.  That's got to

      12      be part of this equation.

      13             And, for the industry not to be represented

      14      today, I can tell you that these questions, if it's

      15      up to me -- and I won't speak for the other senators

      16      because they do a good enough job themselves -- but,

      17      before we allow a multi-billion dollar industry,

      18      that's on the gateway of New York's border, to come

      19      in here and profit off of our land and our

      20      resources, these questions better get answered.

      21             Senator Andrea Stewart-Cousins joined us.

      22      And I know she'll make a few marks, I'm certain.

      23             And, Senator Krueger.

      24             SENATOR KRUEGER:  Thank you.

      25             Hi.  I'm Liz Krueger, and I'm here from





 

                                                                   8
       1      Manhattan.  And I've been working on educating

       2      myself around the risks of hydrofracking, now, for

       3      several years.

       4             And I'm here to say that the City of New York

       5      is almost universally in agreement that the State

       6      should not rush forward with hydrofracking.  And, in

       7      fact, in the Governor's plan, there will be no

       8      hydrofracking in the New York City reservoir areas,

       9      nor the Syracuse reservoir areas.

      10             But, that's not satisfactory.

      11             Simply saying, "Well, we won't put the water

      12      for New York City at risk, but we can ignore what

      13      the questions are for the rest of the state," is not

      14      acceptable.

      15             It's not acceptable to me.  It's not

      16      acceptable to the people of New York City.

      17             I hear, over and over again, from advocates

      18      for the environment, from activists throughout the

      19      state of New York, that they're really scared.

      20             They've seen what happened in Pennsylvania.

      21      They've read the newspaper stories.  They've heard

      22      about the industry being caught lying.  They've

      23      heard about the federal government burying some

      24      reports that aren't so favorable to hydrofracking.

      25             And they're asking us, as state legislators,





 

                                                                   9
       1      they're asking us as their state government, to do

       2      more than our due diligence.  To, cross every "T,"

       3      dot every "I," challenge every assumption, before

       4      any kind of permitting goes forward in New York

       5      State.

       6             I, in fact, am not convinced that there is a

       7      safe way to do this at this point in history.

       8             I'll accept the fact that technology keeps

       9      moving forward, and we might find ways to do

      10      hydrofracking or some other model of removal of

      11      natural gas from below the Marcellus Shale in the

      12      future that doesn't pit our communities at risk, our

      13      air and water at risk, our farm land at risk.

      14             But, based on all of the research I've done,

      15      I don't believe that model exists yet.  And, so, I'm

      16      not supporting New York State going forward with any

      17      permitting at this time.

      18             And I just want to --

      19                  [Applause.]

      20             SENATOR KRUEGER:  Thank you.

      21             -- reinforce what Senator Ball said, when he

      22      pointed out, the industry was invited to this

      23      hearing.  He made it very clear to me that the

      24      industry was invited.

      25             If they've got nothing to hide, why do they





 

                                                                   10
       1      never show up to testify on their own defense?

       2                  [Applause.]

       3             SENATOR KRUEGER:  Look at all of you, you're

       4      here today.

       5                  [Applause.]

       6             SENATOR KRUEGER:  So, I look forward to

       7      hearing from all of you.

       8             And I wish that there was a more honest

       9      dialogue taking place with the people who are

      10      pushing for New York State to allow hydrofracking to

      11      take place.

      12                Thank you, Senator Ball.

      13             SENATOR BALL:  Senator?

      14             SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:  Thank you.

      15             Good morning, everyone.

      16             I'm Senator Andrea Stewart-Cousins.

      17             And, I'm just a little south of Senator Ball,

      18      and a little north of Senator Krueger, but, I think

      19      that the sentiments that have been expressed by my

      20      colleagues have been quite eloquent and quite on

      21      point.

      22             Again, Senator Ball, I thank you for hosting

      23      the hearing.

      24             When I was driving up, I was telling someone

      25      who I respect a great deal, that I was coming to the





 

                                                                   11
       1      fracking hearing.

       2             And she said to me:  Well, you know, I think

       3      that, you know, there's been such a great increase

       4      in the technology, and it's not like it was before.

       5      It's much safer now.  And they go through so many

       6      different things to make sure they protect the water

       7      and the area.

       8             And I said:  You know, maybe you should come

       9      to testify, because, the people who you're getting

      10      this information from, apparently, are depending on,

      11      you, who have no knowledge -- smart lady, wonderful

      12      woman -- but no real knowledge.  But, I, guess

      13      they're depending on "you" to tell "us" that

      14      everything's okay.

      15             And I said:  The fact that they're unwilling

      16      to come, to tell us how everything has improved

      17      makes me, not only suspect, but extremely concerned.

      18             I have always been a legislator that has been

      19      willing to listen to all sides before I rush to

      20      judgment.

      21             I certainly support the moratorium.  And

      22      certainly support the identification of what you're

      23      talking about is in these fracking fluids.

      24             I want a longer time period for discussion on

      25      the DEC.





 

                                                                   12
       1                  [Applause.]

       2             SENATOR STEWART-COUSINS:  60 days is not

       3      enough.

       4             So -- but, but, but, I'm wanting all that,

       5      because I want like you want: to be educated, and

       6      assured.

       7             And when we come to a hearing like this, and

       8      the side that is discussing how beneficial this is

       9      going to be, how it's going to be a win-win-win,

      10      isn't represented, I think it is really sad because

      11      it was a missed opportunity.  And, of course, allows

      12      us to continue to say, you know, "No frackin' way."

      13             But, anyway, I look forward to hearing from

      14      you.

      15             SENATOR BALL:  Okay, well, thank you very

      16      much.

      17             And, we're going to get started.

      18             I do ask, that, if those who are in

      19      attendance can just make sure that we maintain

      20      complete decorum, so we can get through this, and

      21      pay the most respect to those who are speaking.

      22             So, without further ado, Robert Moore,

      23      Environmental Advocates of New York.

      24             Thanks.

      25             ROBERT MOORE:  Thank you very much, Senator.





 

                                                                   13
       1             And thank you, Senator Krueger and

       2      Senator Stewart-Cousins, for also attending this

       3      very important public hearing on the -- one of the

       4      most pressing environmental issues, and one of the

       5      most pressing, I think, economic and

       6      community-development issues facing New York State

       7      today.

       8             In addition, thank you for inviting the other

       9      panelists here today.  They represent a great number

      10      of experts on these issues; the various aspects of

      11      hydrofracking that are going to impact New York

      12      State, potentially, and also concerned members of

      13      New York State's advocacy community.

      14             I am Robert Moore, the executive director of

      15      Environmental Advocates of New York.

      16             Our mission is to protect the air, land,

      17      water, and wildlife, and the health of all

      18      New Yorkers.

      19             We're based in Albany, and we are well known

      20      within the state capital.

      21             We monitor state government, evaluating

      22      proposed laws, and championing the policies and

      23      practices that will ensure the responsible

      24      stewardship of our shared environment.

      25             Today, based on the gas industry's record in





 

                                                                   14
       1      Pennsylvania, Texas, and the many other states where

       2      it has deployed fracking, Environmental Advocates

       3      has well-founded concerns about the ability of the

       4      gas industry to frack without putting our

       5      communities and our waters at risk.

       6             We're also very concerned about the ability

       7      of a depleted state environmental agency to properly

       8      oversee an industry known nationwide for playing

       9      fast-and-loose with the rules.

      10             We also remain deeply concerned that New York

      11      is poised to allow fracking to occur before

      12      developing the proper laws, rules, and regulations,

      13      and enforcement resources, to oversee an industry

      14      whose activities could grow exponentially once it is

      15      allowed to begin operating within our state.

      16             Many of the others testifying here today can

      17      speak to the risks associated with fracking; the

      18      negative impacts it could have on air and water

      19      resource and the questionable economic benefits to

      20      local communities.

      21             I will, therefore, like to -- would like to

      22      focus my testimony on the problems we see with the

      23      process by which New York seems to have embarked

      24      upon to rush to approve gas drilling, as well as

      25      share with those here today, some background on the





 

                                                                   15
       1      activities of the recently convened

       2      Fracking Advisory Panel to the Department of

       3      Environmental Conservation, which I currently serve

       4      upon.

       5             Let me first start by reminding those in

       6      attendance, that Governor Mario -- excuse me --

       7                  [Laughter, and applause.]

       8             ROBERT MOORE:  Although I'm sure

       9      Governor Mario Cuomo would also agree with this

      10      statement, but Governor Andrew Cuomo has repeatedly

      11      said that he would only allow fracking in

      12      New York State if it could be done safely.

      13             He has also said that he intends for the

      14      State's actions be guided by the best available

      15      science.

      16             However, as we sit here today, the Governor

      17      and his administration seem to be deviating from

      18      that course.

      19             At the urging of the Governor's office, the

      20      DEC released in July an incomplete revision of its

      21      plans for allow hydrofracking.  This document, so

      22      eloquently known as "The Predraft Supplemental

      23      Generic Environmental Impact Statement," and for the

      24      sake of brevity, I will simply refer to this as

      25      "The Administration's Draft Drilling Plan" today.





 

                                                                   16
       1             The Cuomo Administration's draft drilling

       2      plan has improved from Governor Paterson's original

       3      plan, but still contains many flaws.  Some of these

       4      flaws are highlighted in a document that I have

       5      attached to my testimony today, which was a

       6      press release from Environmental Advocates and many

       7      other organizations represented here today, of the

       8      ten, kind of, top fracking flaws we saw in this

       9      preliminary draft.

      10             Others will speak more directly to these

      11      flaws associated with the draft drilling plan and

      12      the inherent risks associated with fracking.

      13             DEC Commissioner Joe Martens has stated that

      14      the official public comment period for the

      15      administration's draft drilling plan will begin at

      16      the end of this month.

      17             I would guess, it would probably be the

      18      Friday before Labor Day, if past timing of

      19      public-comment-periods starts is any indication.

      20             Pending the completion -- this is also

      21      pending the completion of an analysis of the

      22      socioeconomic impacts that will be incorporated into

      23      the final plan.

      24             It is the Administration's intent to only

      25      allow a brief 60-day public comment period on this





 

                                                                   17
       1      highly technical 800-plus-page document.

       2             A 60-day public-comment period is holy

       3      inadequate, and we are asking for a 180-day

       4      public-comment period, as many of the people here

       5      today have called for --

       6                  [Applause.]

       7             ROBERT MOORE:   -- as have many of the public

       8      officials that we are speaking with today.

       9             This would allow the public, members of the

      10      legislature, and anybody with a vested interest in

      11      clean water, clean air, and our local communities,

      12      to make sure they have adequate time to review the

      13      draft drilling plan.

      14             Natural gas has been trapped in these shale

      15      deposits for millions of years, so a 180-day comment

      16      period is not going to impact the amount of gas that

      17      can -- continues to be contained in these shale

      18      deposits; nor will it impinge on any reputable

      19      company's ability to extract it if New York decided

      20      to allow them to move forward.

      21             On a separate track from the review of the

      22      draft drilling plan, is also -- are the

      23      deliberations of the DEC's Fracking Advisory Panel,

      24      which as I said before, I'm a member of.

      25             It had its first meeting last -- just last





 

                                                                   18
       1      Thursday.

       2             And the charge of this advisory panel is to:

       3             One: Recommend what resources and staffing

       4      are necessary to provide proper oversight of the gas

       5      industry, should Governor Cuomo decide to move ahead

       6      with fracking;

       7             Two: Recommend how the state should pay for

       8      the dramatic increase in the Department of

       9      Environmental Conservation's resources and staffing,

      10      to carry out that plan;

      11             And, three: Recommend how the state could

      12      generate revenues from natural-gas drilling, and

      13      pass some of these revenues back to local

      14      communities.

      15             The Fracking Advisory Panel is being asked to

      16      make these recommendations before November 1st.

      17      These recommendations will then be used to advise

      18      the Governor's 2012-'13 Executive Budget proposal.

      19             And, therein lies the major problem with the

      20      task before the Advisory Panel.

      21             Once an executive budget is proposed in

      22      January, probably before the end of the requested

      23      180-day public-comment period, and partial review of

      24      public comments, and any alteration of the

      25      administration's drilling plans, becomes extremely





 

                                                                   19
       1      difficult.

       2             Drilling, perhaps, becomes inevitable, and

       3      the approval of permits for drilling almost

       4      predestined.

       5             The reason for this, is that, once the state

       6      includes a proposal for generating revenues from

       7      fracking in the state budget, there is also a plan

       8      for spending those monies.

       9             If the DEC later determined that there's a

      10      need for further study, a need for additional

      11      investigation, or that permits could not be issued

      12      before a more detailed statutory guidance or

      13      regulatory guidance were developed and adopted, the

      14      state financial plan would then be in deficit.

      15      There would be a hole in the state budget, and

      16      budget cuts would then have to be implemented in

      17      order to account for the lack of revenue from not

      18      issuing fracking permits or not collecting receipts

      19      on a production tax or severance tax.

      20             Put more simply:  If Governor Cuomo's next

      21      budget includes revenues associated with fracking,

      22      he's simply counting his chickens before they're

      23      hatched.

      24             Doing so would, in effect, put tremendous

      25      pressure on the DEC to simply approve the





 

                                                                   20
       1      Administration's drilling plan without further

       2      review, without further investigation, without

       3      further consideration of policy options.

       4             In other words:  Planning for the state to

       5      make money from fracking could take the decision on

       6      whether to allow fracking, as well as, when to allow

       7      fracking, and under what conditions fracking might

       8      go forward, out of the DEC's hands in many ways.

       9             Environmental Advocates has clearly stated

      10      this concern to the Fracking Advisory Panel, and

      11      feel it is premature and completely inappropriate to

      12      make a formal recommendation on fracking revenues

      13      until the right policies are in place.

      14             We would urge the State Senate to reject any

      15      budget proposal that includes state revenues from

      16      hydrofracking.

      17             The other two questions before the

      18      Fracking Advisory panel concern the DEC itself, and

      19      how it is funded.

      20             It is important to remember that the DEC has

      21      fewer staff today than at any time since

      22      Governor Mario Cuomo was in office.

      23             Since April of 2008, the agency has now lost

      24      20 percent of its staff.  And its budget for

      25      activities, like, field inspections, air- and





 

                                                                   21
       1      water-quality monitoring, drinking-water testing,

       2      and wildlife studies, and many other activities,

       3      that are central to regulating fracking and

       4      pollution of all types, as well as just monitoring,

       5      the environmental condition, environmental health,

       6      of the state, those budgets have been slashed by

       7      50 percent.

       8             This is an agency in crisis, and unable to

       9      fulfill many of its already-existing

      10      responsibilities.

      11             For this agency to be able to have adequate

      12      staff and resources available to oversee a massive

      13      expansion of fracking in New York State, and the

      14      enormous expansion of DEC responsibilities that

      15      would accompany it, it would not surprise me if DEC

      16      would need a short-term doubling of its resources.

      17             Last week, the Fracking Advisory Panel

      18      received a briefing from agency staff on the scope

      19      of the potential increased responsibilities, should

      20      the Administration's drilling plan be finalized.

      21      And, the scale of the task before them is daunting

      22      to say the least.

      23             Hundreds of new DEC staff would need to be

      24      hired in the next two to three years in order to

      25      meet the projected demands for drilling permits.





 

                                                                   22
       1             On the technology front, the agency is using

       2      antiquated databases and some of the best technology

       3      from the 1980s for tracking and issuing pollution

       4      permits of all types.

       5             And, these would need to be completely

       6      replaced in order to handle the magnified workload

       7      that would be presented if we moved forward with

       8      fracking.

       9             And, the agency does not have the equipment

      10      or manpower necessary to monitor air- or

      11      water-quality impacts associated with fracking.

      12      Indeed, it does not have adequate resources to

      13      monitor the current condition of the state's air

      14      quality and water quality.

      15             I could go on and on with examples of just

      16      how unprepared the DEC is to take on this task at

      17      present.

      18             And, this is but one of many agencies that

      19      needs to oversee aspects of hydrofracking.

      20             The Public Service Commission is going to see

      21      an enormous jump in proposals for the citing of

      22      natural-gas pipelines.

      23             We've had absolutely no discussion of what

      24      additional resources that agency is needing to get.

      25             The Department of Transportation, we already





 

                                                                   23
       1      know, is looking at very severe problems with

       2      maintaining roads and bridge infrastructure in the

       3      state because of increased truck traffic associated

       4      exclusively with hydrofracking.

       5             That information was displayed in a memo from

       6      the Department of Transportation that received press

       7      coverage not too long ago.

       8             There are many agencies that need to be

       9      brought into this process, and to the best of our

      10      knowledge, haven't even been engaged yet.

      11             It's imperative that Governor Cuomo also look

      12      more carefully at the impacts fracking would have on

      13      the workload of a broader state and local government

      14      agencies.

      15             In closing, let me remind those here today,

      16      that Governor Cuomo has committed to the people of

      17      New York State that fracking would only be allowed

      18      if it could be done safely.

      19             He did not say that it would be done as

      20      safely as DEC could regulate it with its current

      21      resources or with available resources.

      22             He did not say it would be done as safely as

      23      was cost-effective for the gas industry.

      24             He said, he would ensure that New Yorkers

      25      would be safe.





 

                                                                   24
       1             However, the process that New York is about
